# The Museum of Almost Nothing

The museum stood between a locksmith and a shop that had been going out of business for eleven years. Its window contained a blue cup, a railway ticket, and a card bearing the words PLEASE DO NOT EXPECT TOO MUCH.

I had passed it twice a day for six months before going inside. By then, I had been appointed to the municipal department responsible for buildings that no longer justified themselves. This was not its official name, but it described our work more accurately than Property Review and Transitional Use.

The museum was scheduled to become a turning lane.

Inside, a woman sat at a desk repairing the elbow of a gray sweater. Behind her stood three glass cabinets, a coat rack, and a grandfather clock without hands.

“Admission?” I asked.

“Optional.”

“How much?”

“Also optional.”

I showed her my identification.

“Oh,” she said. “Then I suppose you’re here about the future.”

She folded the sweater so that the damaged elbow disappeared.

Her name was Mrs. Vale. She did not offer a first name, and I never found an appropriate moment to ask for one. Some people introduce themselves with a small, firmly shut gate around them.

I explained that the city needed an inventory of the collection before the lease could be terminated. Any items of historical significance might qualify for transfer to the regional archive.

Mrs. Vale listened without interrupting.

“What counts as historical significance?” she asked.

“An association with notable people or events. Rarity. Representative value.”

“Representative of what?”

“A period. A way of life.”

She considered this.

“Well,” she said, “everything here is representative of somebody having a day.”

I wrote *mixed domestic artifacts* on my form.

We agreed I would return the following morning with labels, packing materials, and a better pen.

***

The first object was the blue cup from the window.

It was ordinary stoneware, thick at the rim, with a chip beside the handle. A pale line crossed its base where it had once been broken and glued together.

“Provenance?” I asked.

“Kitchen cupboard, mostly.”

“I mean its history.”

“A man named Leonard Pike drank tea from it every morning for thirty-four years. His wife gave it to us after he died.”

“Was he locally prominent?”

“He knew when to put the bins out on holiday weeks.”

I waited.

“That is a form of prominence,” Mrs. Vale said.

I examined the cup for a maker’s mark.

“Why did she donate it?”

“She said the rest of his belongings looked abandoned. The cup looked as though it was waiting.”

There was no field on my form for that distinction.

I recorded its dimensions and condition. Mrs. Vale watched me measure the handle with a folding ruler.

“You’re very careful,” she said.

“It’s the job.”

“No,” she said. “The job would allow considerably less.”

I had no answer prepared for a compliment that sounded like an accusation.

The railway ticket was easier to classify. It had been issued forty-two years earlier for a journey to the coast and punched by a conductor.

“Who traveled?”

“No one.”

“But it’s punched.”

“The donor boarded, changed her mind, and got off before departure.”

“Why?”

“She didn’t tell me.”

I looked again at the faded date.

“Did you ask?”

“Of course. I’m not a saint. She said she preferred not to explain.”

“So you accepted it without knowing the story?”

“I know the story. She bought a ticket. She boarded a train. She got off.”

“That seems incomplete.”

“Only if you insist she should have gone somewhere.”

By eleven, I had cataloged a bent teaspoon, a child’s left mitten, a receipt for twelve oranges, and a small stone described as *possibly from Greece*.

The museum’s founding document occupied a frame beside the desk. It was a letter from the former proprietor of the locksmith’s shop, granting Mrs. Vale use of the adjoining premises for a nominal rent.

“What made you start?”

“I had the room.”

“You must have had some purpose.”

“I thought people might bring things.”

“And did they?”

She gestured toward the cabinets.

“Not in the quantities one might fear.”

At noon, she offered me tea in a cup considerably less interesting than Leonard Pike’s.

I had intended to work through lunch, but the kettle was already boiling. From the street came the hammering of someone assembling metal shelving in the shop next door.

For a moment, neither of us had anything requiring explanation.

***

Over the next week, the inventory advanced slowly.

There were objects whose importance depended entirely upon an accompanying sentence. A plain brass key had once been carried for nineteen years after the door it opened was removed. A wooden ruler belonged to a dressmaker who refused to measure children’s heights against a wall because, she said, growing was not damage. Three buttons had been recovered from the filter of a washing machine on the morning its owner decided to leave her husband.

“Did the buttons influence the decision?” I asked.

“Apparently they were the last straw.”

“How?”

“I didn’t understand. I believe you would have had to know the husband.”

Other objects resisted even that much interpretation.

There was an envelope containing a little dry mud. A bicycle bell that produced a dull click. A photograph of six people, all looking at someone outside the frame.

Mrs. Vale knew the names of only four.

“Doesn’t that bother you?”

“Yes.”

“Can’t you find out?”

“Probably. The donor gave me a number for her cousin.”

“Have you called?”

“No.”

“Why not?”

“She lives in Canada. I keep remembering at the wrong time.”

It was the first wholly practical failure she had admitted. I found it reassuring.

On Thursday, a boy arrived carrying a cracked plastic dinosaur.

He placed it on the desk with the solemnity of someone handing over evidence.

“My brother says you take old stuff.”

“Sometimes,” Mrs. Vale said.

“It’s old.”

“How old?”

“I got it when I was four.”

“How old are you now?”

“Seven.”

“A substantial portion of your life.”

The boy nodded, pleased to find a competent authority.

Mrs. Vale turned the dinosaur over. One foot was missing, and the tail had been repaired with green electrical tape.

“Why don’t you want it anymore?”

“I do want it.”

“Then why bring it here?”

He looked toward the window.

“My brother says if you give something to a museum, they have to keep it forever.”

She put the dinosaur back in his hands.

“We’re not that kind of museum.”

“What kind are you?”

“The kind with a leaking roof.”

The boy considered this information.

“You could put a bucket.”

“We have.”

“Then it should be okay.”

After he left, I asked whether she had always refused gifts from children.

“Only the things they’re trying not to lose.”

That evening, I stayed late at the office to enter the records. Our database required an estimated monetary value for every item. Zero was not accepted. The software interpreted it as an omission.

I valued each object at one unit of currency.

The entire collection came to less than the folding ruler.

***

My supervisor visited on Monday.

He was a tidy man named Bell who could make even good news sound like an adjustment to parking regulations. He walked through the museum without removing his coat.

“How much longer?”

“Three days.”

“You said three days last week.”

“There are more objects than expected.”

He glanced at the nearly empty cabinets.

“Are there?”

“Several drawers.”

Mrs. Vale sat at her desk, working on the same sweater.

Bell lowered his voice.

“We’re not obliged to create a transfer case for every spoon.”

“I know.”

“The archive has storage constraints.”

“I know.”

He looked toward the blue cup.

“Anything valuable?”

“Not financially.”

“That wasn’t my question.”

For the first time, I realized he was asking honestly. I had been preparing to dislike him, which was considerably simpler.

“I haven’t decided,” I said.

“Well, decide by Friday.”

After he left, Mrs. Vale opened the bottom drawer of her desk.

“This one will complicate matters.”

She handed me a square of wallpaper patterned with yellow pears. A narrow strip along one edge was darker than the rest.

“My kitchen,” she said. “Behind the calendar.”

I waited.

“When my husband died, my daughter came to stay. She said we should change something. Not everything. Just something small enough to manage. We took down the wallpaper.”

“Did it help?”

“It needed doing.”

She rubbed a thumb over the dark edge.

“I kept that piece because I liked the pears. Later, I couldn’t remember whether I had liked them before.”

It was the first object she had identified as her own.

“Will you take it with you?”

“I haven’t decided.”

“You don’t have to donate your own things.”

“I’m aware of the distinction.”

But she said it mildly, and left the paper beside my forms.

That afternoon, rain began to fall through the ceiling into a saucepan near the clock. Each drop made a different sound depending on where it struck. Mrs. Vale moved the saucepan twice before appearing satisfied.

I asked about the clock.

“It came with the room.”

“Did it ever work?”

“Certainly.”

“What happened to the hands?”

“I took them off.”

“Why?”

“The mechanism was unreliable. People kept missing buses.”

“Why not stop it?”

“I like the ticking.”

We stood beside it and listened.

Without hands, the sound seemed less supervisory.

On my way home, I missed my bus anyway.

I walked the forty minutes to my apartment through streets that looked briefly unfamiliar in the rain. In a lighted kitchen, someone shook a tablecloth out of a window. A man stood beneath an awning reading instructions on a packet. Outside the pharmacy, two women were laughing so hard that one had to lean against the wall.

I wondered what, if anything, they would keep from that day.

***

On Friday, I brought packing boxes.

Mrs. Vale had cleaned the cabinets. Their glass shelves were so clear that several objects appeared unsupported.

“I’ve spoken to the archive,” I said.

“And?”

“They can take the photograph, the railway ticket, and the founding letter. Possibly the dressmaker’s ruler.”

“Why possibly?”

“They already have rulers.”

“I imagine they do.”

I laid out the other options. Donors could reclaim objects. Unclaimed items could be transferred to a charity shop, disposed of, or retained privately.

“Disposed of,” she repeated.

“It’s the wording on the form.”

“Yes. I wasn’t blaming you for inventing it.”

We worked quietly.

Once removed from the cabinets, the collection looked disconcertingly like the contents of a drawer emptied during a hurried move. Tape snagged on the bicycle bell. The stone from possibly Greece rolled beneath the desk.

I crawled after it and found a cough sweet, two paper clips, and a dried beetle.

“Accession those?” I asked.

Mrs. Vale laughed.

It was the first time I had heard her do so, and I was surprised by its untidiness.

Around noon, the boy returned.

He was not carrying the dinosaur. He brought a cardboard box containing a white kitchen timer.

“This doesn’t work,” he announced.

“What happened to it?”

“My gran dropped it in soup.”

Mrs. Vale lifted it from the box.

“What kind of soup?”

He frowned.

“Does that matter?”

“Not necessarily.”

“Tomato, I think.”

She turned the dial. The timer gave a brief, gritty buzz.

“Does your grandmother know you’ve brought this?”

“She said good riddance.”

“A clear statement of intent.”

The boy noticed the empty shelves.

“Where’s everything going?”

“Different places,” she said.

“Are you moving?”

“The museum is closing.”

He looked at me, then at the boxes.

“Because of the roof?”

“Among other things.”

He took the timer back.

“I’ll keep it till you open again.”

Mrs. Vale began to explain, then stopped.

“All right,” she said.

After he had gone, she sat down heavily.

I continued wrapping the cup.

I had developed an unreasonable wish to save the museum. I imagined petitions, newspaper photographs, a committee in which I would speak more forcefully than I ever did at actual meetings.

But the turning lane was part of a plan to reroute buses past the hospital. The present arrangement required passengers to cross two busy roads. I had seen people attempt it with crutches.

I could not make the museum innocent by making the road cruel.

“What will you do?” I asked.

“My daughter wants me nearer her.”

“Will you go?”

“Probably.”

“And the collection?”

She looked around the room.

“I’ve been keeping some of these things longer than the people who gave them to me.”

“That doesn’t answer the question.”

“No,” she said. “I suppose it doesn’t.”

***

The museum closed on a Wednesday without ceremony.

Three donors reclaimed their possessions. The archive collected its four approved objects. Mrs. Vale kept the wallpaper, the cup, and a box she would not let me inspect.

The rest went to the charity shop, where the bicycle bell sold almost immediately.

Bell signed the paperwork. He thanked me for being thorough.

Six months later, I found the grandfather clock in the locksmith’s window. Its hands had been replaced.

Inside, the locksmith was cutting a key.

“You fixed it,” I said.

“Nothing much wrong with it.”

“Does it keep good time?”

“Near enough. You interested?”

I almost bought it. Instead, I asked whether he had heard from Mrs. Vale.

“Postcard last week. She’s joined a swimming group.”

He pointed to the card beside his till. On the front was an indoor pool. On the back she had written, *Water warmer than expected.*

The bus arrived outside the hospital. Through the window, I watched its doors open toward the pavement.

Then the locksmith handed me Mrs. Vale’s address, written on a clean paper bag. I folded it carefully and put it in my pocket.
